titles: The Man Who Gave the Ponzi Scheme Its Name
Charles Ponzi: 50% in 90 Days, and Who Paid It
How Charles Ponzi Took $2.5 Million in One Month
thumbnail_prompt: Stylized cinematic illustration of a faceless 1920s man in a straw boater hat and three-piece suit, silhouetted beside a closet overflowing with banknotes stacked to the ceiling, single warm gold light, near-black background, empty dark left third, moody film grain
description:
The original Ponzi scheme: in 1920, Charles Ponzi promised Boston fifty percent in ninety days, and thousands lined up to hand him their savings.

It started with an international reply coupon in a letter from Spain and $150. By June 1920, 7,824 people had paid in about $2.5 million in a single month, and his clerks were stacking cash in closets to the ceiling. Then a newspaper started asking questions, and in three days $1.7 million left his bank account.

This is the story of the man whose name became the word for this kind of fraud: the run on his notes, the guilty plea, the investors who got back cents on the dollar, and the warning signs that were there from the start.

shorts.title: From $150 to Cash Stacked to the Ceiling

shorts.title: The Run That Broke Charles Ponzi
shorts.why: Withdrawals pile up, the forgery past comes out, and it ends with Ponzi's line to the reporter and his arrest.

shorts.title: The Real Sign of a Ponzi Scheme
shorts.hook: It paid. That was the problem.
shorts.why: Moves from the sentence and the losses to the channel's own warning signs, ending on a closing line people will want to share.

pinned_comment: Ponzi's early investors really did get paid, often in 45 days. If your neighbour showed you their returns, would you have joined the line in July 1920, or held back? What would have tipped you off?
